Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Conflict: Confrontations, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Vignette:
Caleb Vance was twenty-four when the desert wind carried the taste of copper and burnt cordite into his mouth. He had been standing near a convoy checkpoint when the usual quiet of the forward operating base shattered. It wasn’t a normal lull; it was the heavy, waiting stillness that always preceded an ambush. Then came the shouting, the sudden roar of small arms, and the frantic scramble for cover. He remembered the taste lingering on his tongue, thick and metallic, long after the firefight ended. In those moments, every raised voice, every tactical briefing about choke points and contingencies, felt like it might instantly pull him back to that stretch of sand. When he returned home, the quiet of his own house felt wrong. Silence wasn’t peace anymore; it was the pause before something dangerous arrived. At thirty-six, working as a tax consultant, he spent his days in glass-walled conference rooms with clients whose deductions they questioned. The firm’s climate control kept the air still, but Caleb could feel his stomach tighten whenever a discrepancy was pointed out across the polished mahogany table. He noticed how his eyes constantly tracked the exits, mapping every door and corridor before he would let himself settle into a chair. When a client or a colleague approached him from behind, his shoulders would lock, his breath catching in his throat as his body braced for impact. He had stopped accepting handshakes altogether. Even his wife’s casual attempt to rest her hand on his arm made him jump, his nerves firing alarms he couldn’t control. Over the months, his avoidance took root. He didn’t talk about the deployment, not with his wife, not with his commander, not with anyone. When conversations drifted toward military life or current conflicts, he would change the subject or step away. Positive moments felt precarious. When his wife celebrated an anniversary or laughed at a joke, he would consciously pull back, telling himself it was better to stay guarded. He couldn’t explain why joy felt unsafe, only that the feeling sat heavy in his chest whenever it arose. He also noticed that sudden bouts of nausea often arrived alongside the memories. He had to stop mid-sentence, gripping the edge of a desk or the doorframe, because the emotion hit him so violently he could barely breathe. Sometimes, though, the memories came differently. He would remember the checkpoint, the orders, the radio chatter, but he felt nothing. It was like reading a report written by a stranger. Across the polished mahogany table, he would watch his wife’s mouth move during dinner, the words registering but never quite landing, because his mind kept pacing the perimeter of the room, waiting for the next disruption. Now, in his current office, Caleb sat across from a client whose tone had sharpened during a disagreement over a complex audit. The man’s voice rose, and Caleb’s pulse spiked. He forced himself to stay seated, his eyes flicking instinctively to the double doors at the back of the room. He knew he couldn’t keep mapping exits or swallowing the metallic taste of dread that surfaced whenever tension rose. He had come to believe that staying quiet and keeping his distance was the only way to keep his family and his work intact, but the strain was fracturing both. He was finally sitting in a therapist’s office because his wife had left a stack of unopened bills on the kitchen counter and stopped speaking to him for three days. What frightened him most was that the silence had returned, this time in his own home, and he no longer knew how to step out of it. He hoped someone could help him understand why his own life felt so dangerous to live.
